question: Adult BLS compression-to-ventilation ratio with 2 rescuers:
explanation:
• For adults the compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30:2 with either one or two rescuers, until an advanced airway is placed.
• 15:2 is the two-rescuer ratio for infants and children, not adults, and 5:1 was withdrawn from the guidelines in 2005.
• Once an advanced airway is in situ, compressions become continuous at 100-120/min with one breath every 6 seconds.
citation: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and ECC (2020)

question: Adult compression depth (approx):
explanation:
• Adult chest compressions must be at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep, and not more than 2.4 inches (6 cm), delivered at 100-120 per minute with full recoil between compressions.
• 1 inch or 3 cm is too shallow to generate the coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure needed to sustain the brain and myocardium.
• Deliberately shallow compressions are never correct; the depth limit exists only to avoid rib and visceral injury, not to justify under-compressing.
citation: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and ECC (2020)

question: Rule of Nines: adult anterior trunk is about:
explanation:
• In the adult Rule of Nines the trunk is 36% of body surface area, divided as 18% anterior and 18% posterior.
• 9% applies to each upper limb and to the head and neck, while each lower limb is 18%.
• 36% is the whole trunk (front plus back), so it overstates the anterior surface alone, and 27% is not a Rule of Nines value at all.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)

question: First-line drug for anaphylaxis:
explanation:
• Intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh (adult dose 0.5 mg of 1:1000) is the first-line, life-saving treatment because it reverses bronchospasm, vasodilatation and capillary leak within minutes.
• Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only: they relieve urticaria or reduce late-phase reactions but act far too slowly to treat airway obstruction or shock.
• Beta blockers are contraindicated because they oppose the action of adrenaline and can deepen hypotension and bronchospasm.
citation: World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidance (2020 update)

question: Typical adult Hb lower limit (female approx):
explanation:
• WHO defines anaemia in non-pregnant adult women as haemoglobin below 12 g/dL, so 12 g/dL is the accepted lower limit of normal.
• The corresponding cut-off is 13 g/dL for adult men and 11 g/dL in pregnancy.
• 10 g/dL and 8 g/dL already represent mild-to-moderate and severe anaemia respectively, while 14 g/dL lies comfortably inside the normal female range rather than at its floor.
citation: WHO, Haemoglobin Concentrations for the Diagnosis of Anaemia and Assessment of Severity (2011)

question: Open fracture priority includes:
options: B. Cover with sterile dressing, immobilize, urgent care
explanation:
• An open (compound) fracture is a surgical emergency: control bleeding, cover the wound with a sterile dressing to limit contamination, immobilise the limb in the position found, and arrange urgent transfer for debridement, antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis.
• Range-of-motion exercises would displace the bone ends, increase bleeding and risk neurovascular injury.
• Massaging the wound drives contamination deeper, and heat increases bleeding and swelling; cold and immobilisation, not heat, are used in acute fracture care.
citation: St John Ambulance / St Andrew's First Aid / British Red Cross, First Aid Manual, 11th ed. (2021)

question: Respiratory acidosis shows:
options: B. High CO2 with acidic pH
explanation:
• Respiratory acidosis is caused by alveolar hypoventilation, so carbon dioxide is retained (PaCO2 above 45 mmHg) and the pH falls below 7.35.
• A low CO2 with a raised pH describes respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation, and a high bicarbonate with alkalaemia is metabolic alkalosis.
• The pH may drift back toward normal once the kidneys compensate by retaining bicarbonate, but it is never invariably normal, which rules out the last option.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)

question: Shockable rhythms in cardiac arrest include:
explanation:
• Only ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are shockable, because defibrillation depolarises the myocardium simultaneously and allows an organised rhythm to resume.
• Asystole and pulseless electrical activity are non-shockable and are managed with high-quality CPR, adrenaline every 3-5 minutes and correction of reversible causes.
• Bradycardia with a pulse is treated with atropine, chronotropic infusion or pacing, never with defibrillation.
citation: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and ECC (2020)

question: Clinical pathology Q9: Platelet count very low increases risk of:
explanation:
• Platelets form the primary haemostatic plug, so a very low count causes bleeding: petechiae, purpura, bleeding gums, epistaxis and, when severe, gastrointestinal or intracranial haemorrhage.
• Thrombosis is the opposite problem and follows platelet excess or activation, not a low count.
• Serum sodium and acid-base balance are regulated by the kidneys and lungs, so hypernatraemia and metabolic alkalosis have no causal link to the platelet count.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)

question: Clinical pathology Q10: Platelet count very low increases risk of:
explanation:
• Spontaneous bleeding risk climbs steeply once the platelet count falls below about 20,000/mm3, and counts under 10,000/mm3 carry a real risk of intracranial and gastrointestinal haemorrhage.
• Because too few platelets means clots cannot form normally, thrombosis is not the expected consequence.
• Hypernatraemia is a water and sodium imbalance and metabolic alkalosis an acid-base disturbance; neither results from thrombocytopenia.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)

question: Clinical pathology Q11: Platelet count very low increases risk of:
explanation:
• Thrombocytopenia (count below 150,000/mm3) prolongs bleeding time and produces mucocutaneous bleeding such as petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis and menorrhagia.
• Nursing management therefore centres on bleeding precautions: soft toothbrush, no intramuscular injections or rectal temperatures, and avoidance of aspirin and NSAIDs.
• The remaining options describe excess clotting and electrolyte or acid-base disorders, none of which follow from a low platelet count.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)

question: Clinical pathology Q12: Platelet count very low increases risk of:
explanation:
• A very low platelet count means the primary haemostatic plug cannot form, so the patient bleeds rather than clots.
• Frequent causes in Indian practice include dengue, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, aplastic anaemia, hypersplenism and chemotherapy-induced marrow suppression.
• Hypernatraemia reflects water and sodium balance and metabolic alkalosis reflects acid-base regulation; neither is produced by thrombocytopenia, and thrombosis is the opposite abnormality.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)

question: Clinical pathology Q13: Platelet count very low increases risk of:
explanation:
• Bleeding is the hallmark of severe thrombocytopenia, because platelets are needed for adhesion, aggregation and the initial plug that seals small vessel breaks.
• The earliest visible signs are usually petechiae and purpura over dependent areas, followed by mucosal bleeding from gums, nose or urinary tract.
• Thrombosis, hypernatraemia and metabolic alkalosis arise from entirely different mechanisms and are not consequences of a falling platelet count.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)

question: Clinical pathology Q14: Platelet count very low increases risk of:
explanation:
• Platelet transfusion is generally considered prophylactically below 10,000/mm3, and below 50,000/mm3 before invasive procedures, precisely because bleeding risk rises as the count falls.
• A deficiency of platelets cannot promote clot formation, so thrombosis is incorrect.
• Sodium concentration and acid-base status are governed by renal and respiratory mechanisms and are unaffected by platelet numbers.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)

question: Clinical pathology Q15: Platelet count very low increases risk of:
explanation:
• Very low platelets are a quantitative defect of primary haemostasis, presenting as prolonged oozing from venepuncture sites, bleeding gums, epistaxis and heavy menstrual loss.
• Clotting factor disorders such as haemophilia instead cause deep muscle and joint bleeds, but both categories present with bleeding rather than clotting.
• Hypernatraemia and metabolic alkalosis are unrelated metabolic disturbances, and thrombosis would suggest platelet excess or hypercoagulability.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)

question: Clinical pathology Q16: Platelet count very low increases risk of:
explanation:
• A severely reduced platelet count leaves small capillary breaches unsealed, so even minor trauma produces disproportionate bruising and prolonged bleeding.
• This is why nurses avoid intramuscular injections, rectal temperatures, razors and hard toothbrushes in thrombocytopenic patients and apply prolonged pressure after any needle stick.
• Thrombosis follows platelet excess or activation, while hypernatraemia and metabolic alkalosis are unrelated electrolyte and acid-base problems.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)

question: Clinical pathology Q17: Platelet count very low increases risk of:
explanation:
• Bleeding is correct because platelets are the cells that plug endothelial gaps; without enough of them, petechiae, purpura and mucosal or intracranial haemorrhage can occur.
• Dengue is a common cause of a rapidly falling count in India and demands close monitoring of both platelet trend and bleeding manifestations.
• Neither hypernatraemia nor metabolic alkalosis is produced by thrombocytopenia, and thrombosis is the opposite haematological abnormality.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)

question: Clinical pathology Q18: Platelet count very low increases risk of:
explanation:
• Thrombocytopenia impairs primary haemostasis and therefore increases bleeding risk, with spontaneous haemorrhage becoming likely below roughly 20,000/mm3.
• Assessment should cover petechiae, bruising, bleeding gums, haematuria, melaena and any fall in level of consciousness that could signal intracranial bleeding.
• Thrombosis, hypernatraemia and metabolic alkalosis have no causal relationship with a low platelet count and are distractors here.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)
